claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the metabolic analysis and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Both chromerids and apicomplexans encode modular multi-domain fatty acid synthase I (FASI)/polyketide synthase enzymes and single-domain FASII components.
claims.source: Both chromerids and apicomplexans encode modular multi-domain fatty acid synthase I (FASI)/polyketide synthase enzymes and single-domain FASII components (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: Treatment of Chromera with a FASII inhibitor triclosan showed decreased production of long chain fatty acids.
claims.source: Treatment of Chromera with a FASII inhibitor triclosan showed decreased production of long chain fatty acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Appendix 2), suggesting that Chromera synthesizes short-chain saturated fatty acids using the FASI pathway, which are then elongated using the FASII pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Chromera synthesizes short-chain saturated fatty acids using the FASI pathway, which are then elongated using the FASII pathway.
claims.source: Treatment of Chromera with a FASII inhibitor triclosan showed decreased production of long chain fatty acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Appendix 2), suggesting that Chromera synthesizes short-chain saturated fatty acids using the FASI pathway, which are then elongated using the FASII pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the triclosan treatment experiment.

claims.claim: Transition to an apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) was accompanied by the loss of metabolic processes including photosynthesis and sterol biosynthesis.
claims.source: Transition to an apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) was accompanied by the loss of metabolic processes including photosynthesis and sterol biosynthesis (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the metabolic pathway analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The apicomplexan ancestor appeared to possess a significant complement of enzymes in various pathways.
claims.source: The apicomplexan ancestor appeared to possess a significant complement of enzymes in various pathways (Figure 2B) (Lim and McFadden, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the metabolic pathway analysis shown in Figure 2B and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The proto-apicomplexan had a nearly complete repertoire of the endomembrane trafficking complexes.
claims.source: The proto-apicomplexan had a nearly complete repertoire of the endomembrane trafficking complexes, and much of this repertoire persisted through to the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) (Hager et al., 1999; Klinger et al., 2013a) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Appendix 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the endomembrane trafficking analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4, and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: All known components of flagella were present in the proto-apicomplexan ancestor.
claims.source: All known components of flagella were present in the proto-apicomplexan ancestor (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B.

claims.claim: Most of the flagellar components were retained in the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II), but losses occurred as apicomplexan lineages differentiated (Stage III).
claims.source: Most of the components were retained in the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II), but losses occurred as apicomplexan lineages differentiated (Stage III).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B.

claims.claim: Components of intraflagellar transport were lost in all apicomplexan lineages except in coccidians.
claims.source: Components of intraflagellar transport, which are typically essential for assembling flagella, were lost in the other lineages except in coccidians (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B.

claims.claim: The basal body proteins were lost from piroplasms.
claims.source: The basal body proteins, which support an organizing center for microtubules, were lost from piroplasms.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis.

claims.claim: Some striated fiber assemblin (SFA) proteins were maintained in all apicomplexan lineages including piroplasms.
claims.source: Some striated fiber assemblin (SFA) proteins, typically associated with basal body rootlets, were maintained in all apicomplexan lineages including piroplasms (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B,D); their presence has been hailed as evidence that some flagellar-proteins are repurposed for new functions in apicomplexans (see below) (Francia et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B,D and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Genes encoding extracellular proteins exported into the host environments were over-represented among those gained after Stage III.
claims.source: Genes encoding extracellular proteins exported into the host environments were over-represented among those gained after Stage III (Figure 3), suggesting that adaptation to specific hosts was accompanied by expansion of extracellular proteins mediating host–parasite interactions (Templeton et al., 2004a; Anantharaman et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary age analysis shown in Figure 3 and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Stage III was accompanied by gains of genes encoding DBD proteins, mostly apiAP2 proteins.
claims.source: Stage III was accompanied by gains of those encoding DBD proteins, mostly apiAP2 proteins (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting extensive regulatory changes mediated by apiAP2 proteins during lineage differentiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary age analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Stage II was accompanied by over-represented gains of various cytoskeletal components, including alveolins, those of the actomyosin complex and glideosome-associated proteins.
claims.source: Stage II was accompanied by over-represented gains of various cytoskeletal components, including alveolins, those of the actomyosin complex (e.g., myosins) and glideosome-associated proteins with multiple membrane spans 1 and 3 (GAPM1 and GAPM3), suggesting that the molecular machinery powering gliding motility, which is essential for host cell invasion arose during evolution to apicomplexans (Frenal et al., 2010) (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Appendix 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary age analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Gene gains during Stage I were over-represented by proteins with 'RBD abundant in Apicomplexans' (RAP).
claims.source: Gene gains during Stage I were over-represented by proteins with 'RBD abundant in Apicomplexans' (RAP, Pfam: PF08373) (Lee and Hong, 2004), many of which were conserved as one-to-one orthologs across descending lineages, suggesting development of evolutionarily conserved functions before apicomplexans and chromerids diverged (Figure 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary age analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Chromerid genomes encode many orthologs of apicomplexan cytoskeletal proteins.
claims.source: Chromerid genomes encode many orthologs of apicomplexan cytoskeletal proteins (Appendix 4), including GAPM2, a member of an important protein family for apicomplexan cytoskeletal structure and gliding motility (Bullen et al., 2009), and the IMC sub-compartment protein family (ISP), implicated in establishing apical polarity and coordinating the unique cell cycle of apicomplexans (Poulin et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Chromerid genomes encode GAPM2, a member of an important protein family for apicomplexan cytoskeletal structure and gliding motility.
claims.source: Chromerid genomes encode many orthologs of apicomplexan cytoskeletal proteins (Appendix 4), including GAPM2, a member of an important protein family for apicomplexan cytoskeletal structure and gliding motility (Bullen et al., 2009), and the IMC sub-compartment protein family (ISP), implicated in establishing apical polarity and coordinating the unique cell cycle of apicomplexans (Poulin et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Chromerid genomes encode the IMC sub-compartment protein family (ISP), implicated in establishing apical polarity and coordinating the unique cell cycle of apicomplexans.
claims.source: Chromerid genomes encode many orthologs of apicomplexan cytoskeletal proteins (Appendix 4), including GAPM2, a member of an important protein family for apicomplexan cytoskeletal structure and gliding motility (Bullen et al., 2009), and the IMC sub-compartment protein family (ISP), implicated in establishing apical polarity and coordinating the unique cell cycle of apicomplexans (Poulin et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Chromerid genomes encode numerous apiAP2 proteins, more abundant than dinoflagellates.
claims.source: Importantly, chromerid genomes encode numerous apiAP2 proteins, more abundant than dinoflagellates, suggesting that they have expanded in the proto-apicomplexan ancestor after it split from dinoflagellates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Many of the chromerid apiAP2 proteins belong to putative paralogous clusters, suggesting that their expansion was driven by gene duplication.
claims.source: Many of the chromerid apiAP2 proteins belong to putative paralogous clusters, suggesting that their expansion was driven by gene duplication (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Appendix 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and is an inference based on the data.

claims.claim: Only a small subset of the apiAP2 proteins are shared across apicomplexans.
claims.source: Only a small subset of the apiAP2 proteins are shared across apicomplexans, suggesting that the large apiAP2 complement in the proto-apicomplexan ancestor has diversified independently in descending lineages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and is an inference based on the data.

claims.claim: For 11 out of 12 orthogroups with RAP domains, co-expressed orthogroups overlapped significantly between P. falciparum and Chromera.
claims.source: For 11 out of 12 orthogroups with RAP domains, co-expressed orthogroups overlapped significantly (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.05) between P. falciparum and Chromera, suggesting involvement of RAP proteins in cellular processes evolutionarily conserved across apicomplexans and chromerids (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: RAP and their co-expressed orthogroups encode proteins with putative mitochondrial import signals more often than expected by chance in Chromera and P. falciparum.
claims.source: RAP and their co-expressed orthogroups encode proteins with putative mitochondrial import signals more often than expected by chance in Chromera and P. falciparum (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.05) (Figure 4B), and also in other apicomplexans and chromerids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the subcellular localization prediction analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Three Toxoplasma RAP genes with predicted mitochondrial localization signals are localized to the mitochondrion.
claims.source: We have randomly chosen three Toxoplasma RAP genes with predicted mitochondrial localization signals (Supplementary file 6) and confirmed experimentally by 3′ endogenous gene-tagging with reporter epitopes that all three are localized to the organelle (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental localization data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The Cryptosporidium lineage that has a highly reduced mitochondrion lacking both the genome and most canonical metabolic pathways is the only apicomplexan group to have also lost its RAP repertoire.
claims.source: Consistent with this, the Cryptosporidium lineage that has a highly reduced mitochondrion lacking both the genome and most canonical metabolic pathways (Abrahamsen et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2004) is the only apicomplexan group to have also lost its RAP repertoire (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The frequency of co-expression amongst 80 orthogroups comprising genes functionally annotated as implicated in invasion processes in the free-living Chromera was significantly higher than expected by chance.
claims.source: Among the 1918 orthogroups, we identified 80 orthogroups comprising genes functionally annotated as implicated in invasion processes. The frequency of co-expression amongst them in the free-living Chromera was significantly higher than expected by chance (p < 0.0005), suggesting pre-existing functional relationships before transitioning to parasites (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: In one of the co-expression modules, 9 out of 10 orthogroups are co-expressed with a gene encoding SFA (Cvel_872).
claims.source: In one of the co-expression modules (numbered 1 in Figures 4E), 9 out of 10 orthogroups are co-expressed with a gene encoding SFA (Cvel_872), a key protein for organizing the basal bodies of the flagellar apparatus in algae and the apical complexes in apicomplexans (Kawase et al., 2007; Francia et al., 2012) (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4E and 4F, and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: SFAs are the only flagellar components found in all apicomplexans tested.
claims.source: We note that SFAs are the only flagellar components found in all apicomplexans tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claims.claim: For 9 out of 10 orthogroups in the co-expression module with SFA, their co-expressed orthogroups in Chromera overlapped significantly with those in P. falciparum.
claims.source: Also in this module, for 9 out of 10 orthogroups, their co-expressed orthogroups in Chromera overlapped significantly with those in P. falciparum (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.05), indicating that their regulatory programs have been evolutionarily conserved (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The co-expression module with SFA includes various types of genes implicated in host cell invasion processes of apicomplexans such as genes encoding rhoptry protein ROP9, apical sushi protein ASP, and gliding motility components GAP40 and GAPM2.
claims.source: This module include various types of genes implicated in host cell invasion processes of apicomplexans such as genes encoding rhoptry protein ROP9, apical sushi protein ASP, and gliding motility components GAP40 and GAPM2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis and functional annotation of genes in the module.

claims.claim: The apical complex has been postulated to have emerged from the flagellar apparatus and associated cellular transport systems in free-living algae, based on ultrastructural evidence.
claims.source: The apical complex has been postulated to have emerged from the flagellar apparatus and associated cellular transport systems in free-living algae, based on ultrastructural evidence (Okamoto and Keeling, 2014; Portman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In the free-living ancestor, some of the genes implicated in the invasion process of present-day apicomplexans were functionally associated with those implicated in flagellar motility.
claims.source: These results suggest that, in the free-living ancestor, some of the genes implicated in the invasion process of present-day apicomplexans were functionally associated with those implicated in flagellar motility, providing the much-needed genetic evidence for the postulate.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the co-expression analysis.

claims.claim: A group of functionally related proteins associated with the flagellar apparatus was repurposed as a module of the apical complex and became a foundation for the invasion machinery.
claims.source: We speculate that a group of functionally related proteins associated with the flagellar apparatus was repurposed as a module of the apical complex and became a foundation for the invasion machinery.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the co-expression analysis and evolutionary inference.

claims.claim: The transition to parasitism was accompanied by massive genomic loss that continued as its descendants became specialized intracellular parasites infecting diverse hosts.
claims.source: Analysis of Chromera and Vitrella genomes has enabled insights into how apicomplexan parasites have evolved from free-living ancestors. The transition to parasitism was accompanied by massive genomic loss that continued as its descendants became specialized intracellular parasites infecting diverse hosts.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the gene gain/loss analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The genome of free-living photosynthetic ancestors encodes many component proteins previously assumed to be restricted to the parasitic apicomplexan lineages.
claims.source: The genome of free-living photosynthetic ancestors encodes many component proteins previously assumed to be restricted to the parasitic apicomplexan lineages.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative genomic analysis showing orthologs of apicomplexan proteins in chromerids.

claims.claim: Pre-existing components in the free-living ancestor, including those of what would later become part of the invasion machinery, were co-opted during evolution to facilitate a successful parasitic lifestyle in multiple hosts.
claims.source: Such pre-existing components, including those of what would later become part of the invasion machinery, were co-opted during evolution to facilitate a successful parasitic lifestyle in multiple hosts.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the comparative genomic and co-expression analyses.

claims.claim: The genome of the proto-apicomplexan ancestor served as a molecular blueprint for evolution of the most successful group of eukaryotic parasites known to date.
claims.source: The genome of the proto-apicomplexan ancestor served as a molecular blueprint for evolution of the most successful group of eukaryotic parasites known to date.
claims.evidence: This is a concluding statement that summarizes the main findings and is an inference based on the entire study.

results.result: The authors sequenced and assembled the nuclear genomes of Chromera velia (193.6 Mb in 5953 scaffolds with 26,112 predicted protein-coding genes) and Vitrella brassicaformis (72.7 Mb in 1064 scaffolds with 22,817 predicted protein-coding genes). The genome size disparity is primarily due to transposable elements (~30 Mb in Chromera vs 1.5 Mb in Vitrella).
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 provide consistent genome assembly statistics supported by the sequencing data presented in the manuscript. The assembly metrics, gene counts, and transposable element content are directly derived from the genomic data and are internally consistent.

results.result: Chromera velia and Vitrella brassicaformis are free-living photosynthetic algae that form a clade closest to Apicomplexa on the phylogenetic tree, confirming the hypothesis that apicomplexan parasites originated from a free-living photosynthetic ancestor. The long phylogenetic branches between the two chromerids reflect substantial differences in their morphology, life cycles, and organellar genomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C14, C15, C21, and C22 are well-supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A, which uses 101 one-to-one orthologs across 26 species with strong bootstrap support (100% for most nodes). The phylogenetic placement is consistent with previous studies cited in the manuscript.

results.result: Gene gain/loss analysis reveals that the transition from the proto-apicomplexan ancestor to the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) involved massive gene loss (3862 orthogroups) with minimal gains (81 orthogroups). Earlier divergence from the alveolate ancestor (Stage I) showed balanced gains (2197) and losses (1668), while subsequent lineage differentiation (Stage III) showed variable patterns: modest changes in coccidians (537 losses, 414 gains) versus drastic losses in hematozoans (1384 losses, 77 gains).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 are supported by the Dollo parsimony analysis shown in Figure 2A and validated by alternative methods (birth-and-death model in Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The quantitative data on orthogroup gains and losses are consistent across different analytical approaches, providing robust support for the evolutionary trajectory.

results.result: The proto-apicomplexan ancestor possessed complete metabolic pathways for sugar metabolism, nitrate/sulfite assimilation, and photosynthesis, including unique features like mitochondrial heme synthesis via the C4 pathway and both FASI and FASII fatty acid synthesis systems. Experimental triclosan treatment of Chromera confirmed FASII function in elongating short-chain fatty acids produced by FASI. The transition to the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) involved loss of photosynthesis and sterol biosynthesis, though significant metabolic capacity was retained.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 are supported by comprehensive metabolic pathway analysis (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and experimental validation (triclosan treatment, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C). The metabolic reconstruction is based on systematic enzyme identification and is consistent with cited literature on apicomplexan metabolism.

results.result: The proto-apicomplexan ancestor possessed a nearly complete repertoire of endomembrane trafficking complexes and all known flagellar components. Most endomembrane and flagellar components persisted through Stage II, but lineage-specific losses occurred during Stage III differentiation. Notably, intraflagellar transport components were lost in all lineages except coccidians, basal body proteins were lost from piroplasms, while striated fiber assemblin (SFA) proteins were maintained across all apicomplexan lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are supported by systematic analysis of endomembrane trafficking components (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and flagellar components (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B). The Dollo parsimony reconstruction provides a clear evolutionary trajectory of component retention and loss across lineages.

results.result: Gene gains at different evolutionary stages show functional specialization: Stage III gains were enriched for extracellular proteins and apiAP2 transcription factors (suggesting host adaptation and regulatory diversification); Stage II gains included cytoskeletal components like alveolins, actomyosin complex proteins, and GAPM1/GAPM3 (invasion machinery); Stage I gains were enriched for RAP domain proteins that became conserved across descending lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by the evolutionary age analysis shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures. The over-representation of specific functional categories at different evolutionary stages is statistically demonstrated and consistent with the proposed evolutionary narrative of parasite adaptation.

results.result: Chromerid genomes encode orthologs of apicomplexan cytoskeletal proteins including GAPM2 (gliding motility) and ISP family proteins (apical polarity), as well as numerous apiAP2 transcription factors (more abundant than in dinoflagellates). Many chromerid apiAP2 proteins belong to paralogous clusters suggesting expansion by gene duplication, though only a small subset of apiAP2 proteins are shared across apicomplexans, indicating independent diversification in descending lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 are supported by genomic analysis and sequence homology networks (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The presence of apicomplexan-like proteins in chromerids is well-documented through orthology analysis, and the paralogous relationships are demonstrated through phylogenetic and network analyses.

results.result: RAP domain proteins show conserved co-expression patterns between Chromera and P. falciparum (11 of 12 orthogroups with significant overlap, p<0.05), with enrichment for mitochondrial targeting signals in both species (p<0.05). Experimental validation confirmed mitochondrial localization of three randomly selected Toxoplasma RAP proteins. Consistent with a mitochondrial role, Cryptosporidium (with highly reduced mitochondria) is the only apicomplexan lineage that lost its RAP repertoire.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by co-expression analysis (Figure 4A,B), subcellular localization predictions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), experimental validation (Figure 4C), and comparative genomics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). The convergence of computational predictions, experimental data, and evolutionary patterns provides strong support for RAP protein function in mitochondria.

results.result: Among 80 orthogroups implicated in apicomplexan invasion processes, co-expression frequency in Chromera was significantly higher than expected by chance (p<0.0005). One co-expression module includes 9 of 10 orthogroups co-expressed with SFA (the only flagellar component found in all apicomplexans), and these show conserved co-expression patterns between Chromera and P. falciparum (9 of 10 with p<0.05). This module includes invasion-related genes (ROP9, ASP, GAP40, GAPM2), suggesting that invasion machinery genes were functionally associated with flagellar motility genes in the free-living ancestor.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 and C61 are supported by co-expression analysis across 36 environmental conditions in Chromera (Figure 4D-G). The statistical significance of co-expression patterns, conservation across species, and functional coherence of the modules provide strong evidence for pre-existing functional relationships that were later co-opted for parasitism.

results.result: The evolution of apicomplexan parasites from free-living ancestors involved progressive, non-random loss of metabolic and endomembrane trafficking proteins associated with free-living lifestyle, while the free-living ancestor's genome contained a broad repertoire of genes (including invasion-related proteins) that were repurposed for parasitic processes. Pre-existing components were co-opted during evolution to facilitate parasitic lifestyle in multiple hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C63-C65 represent the overarching conclusions supported by the comprehensive genomic, metabolic, and co-expression analyses presented throughout the manuscript. The evidence from gene gain/loss analysis, metabolic reconstruction, and co-expression patterns converges to support this evolutionary narrative.

results.result: The authors propose that the apical complex emerged from the flagellar apparatus in free-living algae (citing ultrastructural evidence from prior studies), and speculate that functionally related proteins associated with the flagellar apparatus were repurposed as a module of the apical complex to become the foundation for invasion machinery.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 cites prior ultrastructural studies as support for the hypothesis, while C62 is explicitly speculative. The co-expression data (C55-C59, C61) provide genetic evidence consistent with this hypothesis, but the mechanistic claim of repurposing remains inferential. The authors appropriately frame C62 as speculation, and while the data are suggestive, direct functional evidence for repurposing is not provided.

results.result: Background claims about Apicomplexa (thousands of obligate intracellular parasites with socio-economic impacts; >5000 described species with >1 million estimated to exist) and their unifying features (nucleic acid-binding proteins, extracellular proteins, apical complex, IMC, apicoplast) are established from prior literature. Chromerids are photosynthetic colpodellids associated with corals.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C13 are background statements supported by citations to established literature. These provide context for the study but are not novel findings from this work. The claims accurately represent the current understanding of apicomplexan biology and chromerid ecology based on cited sources.

results.result: The genome of the proto-apicomplexan ancestor served as a molecular blueprint for evolution of the most successful group of eukaryotic parasites known to date.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 is a concluding synthesis statement that summarizes the main findings of the study. It is supported by the comprehensive evidence presented throughout the manuscript showing that the proto-apicomplexan ancestor possessed genes that were later adapted for parasitism. However, the characterization as 'most successful' is somewhat subjective.
